newsitem.title: UK: British doctors stop lung cancer drug trial.
newsitem.headline: British doctors stop lung cancer drug trial.

text.p: British researchers said on Friday they had stopped a study of a hopeful new cancer drug because it was useless.
They said using etoposide tablets alone did not work against small-cell lung cancer, an illness that has frustrated doctors for years because it does not respond to drugs.
Dr David Girling and colleagues at the Medical Research Council were testing etoposide tablets alone versus intravenous etoposide plus other cancer drugs in 339 seriously ill patients.

"Before the planned intake of 450 patients had been completed the trial was stopped on the recommendation of an independent data monitoring committee, because of the inferiority of oral etoposide," they wrote in the Lancet medical journal.

They had hoped etoposide would work against the cancer. But at six months, 35 percent of patients given etoposide were alive, compared to 49 percent of controls given intravenous combinations of drugs.

"The reason why we were doing the trial is because (etoposide tablets are) being increasingly used, because it's so easy to just take a tablet. People should not just use new ways of using drugs like this unless they've been assessed," Girling said.
But Matti Aapro of the European Institute of Oncology in Milan said this did not mean the drug should not be used.
"It is too early to dismiss oral etoposide, since data on quality of life have not been presented in full and data on survival are not quite convincing," Aapro wrote in a commentary in Nature.

"Etoposide is active against many tumour types, and its oral form could well be combined with other oral agents, including topotecan, which when given intravenously is an extremely active agent against small-cell cancer."
Etoposide is made by Bristol-Myers Squibb Co.
